title: 7 Concepts That Sharpen Historical Thinking
dek: The ideas historians use to see patterns, and who argued them

slides.heading: The Longue Durée
slides.body: Fernand Braudel argued that history moves at three speeds: events, cycles and slow structures such as climate, geography and trade routes. In *The Mediterranean* (1949), the sea itself shapes the story more than kings do.

slides.heading: The Sattelzeit
slides.body: Reinhart Koselleck named roughly 1750 to 1850 a 'saddle period', when words like history, revolution and progress took on their modern meanings. The project behind it is *Geschichtliche Grundbegriffe*, edited with Brunner and Conze.

slides.heading: Gresham's Law
slides.body: When two coins share a face value, people spend the debased one and hoard the good one. The name honours Thomas Gresham, but Henry Dunning Macleod coined it in 1858. Oresme and Copernicus described the effect earlier.

slides.heading: The Price Revolution
slides.body: European prices rose several times over between about 1500 and 1650. Earl J. Hamilton blamed American silver in *American Treasure and the Price Revolution in Spain* (1934). Others, including Jack Goldstone, stress population growth. The cause remains contested.

slides.heading: The Pirenne Thesis
slides.body: Henri Pirenne argued in *Mohammed and Charlemagne* (1937) that the Roman economic world survived the barbarians and ended only when Islam split the Mediterranean. Archaeologists such as Hodges and Whitehouse, and later Michael McCormick, have heavily revised it.

slides.heading: Microhistory
slides.body: Reduce the scale and the past gets bigger. Carlo Ginzburg rebuilt the worldview of Menocchio, a Friulian miller tried by the Inquisition, in *The Cheese and the Worms* (1976). Giovanni Levi and Natalie Zemon Davis developed the method.

slides.heading: The Invention of Tradition
slides.body: Many customs that feel ancient are recent. Eric Hobsbawm and Terence Ranger collected the cases in *The Invention of Tradition* (1983), including Hugh Trevor-Roper's essay on how the Highland tradition of Scotland was largely constructed.

cta_line: On the Substack, each of these concepts gets a long essay: where it came from, what it explains, and where it breaks.
caption:
Seven ideas do more work in a historian's head than any list of dates.
Braudel taught us to watch slow structures (Braudel 1949). Koselleck showed that words change meaning (Koselleck 1972). Hamilton and Pirenne made bold arguments that later evidence complicated (Hamilton 1934; McCormick 2001). Ginzburg showed that one miller can open up a whole world (Ginzburg 1976).
Comment READ and I will send you the Substack link.
risk_notes: Editor asked for 'Rules of a Hanseatic merchant', but '8 Rules of a Hanseatic Merchant' is a recent title, so under house rule 6 this post covers the engine's concepts brief instead.
Sattelzeit dates: Koselleck used roughly 1750 to 1850 as an approximate heuristic. Say 'roughly' and point to his introduction to Geschichtliche Grundbegriffe (vol. 1, 1972).
Gresham's law: Gresham did not formulate it as a law. Macleod named it in 1858. Oresme (De moneta) and Copernicus (Monetae cudendae ratio) described the effect earlier. The slide already says this.
Price revolution: the size of the rise varies by region and index. Keep it at 'several times over' and treat silver against population as an open debate.
Pirenne thesis: some scholars defend parts of it. Say 'heavily revised' rather than 'refuted'. Hodges and Whitehouse 1983, McCormick 2001.
Invention of tradition: Trevor-Roper's essay is debated by some Scottish historians. Use 'largely constructed' and attribute it to him.

issues.problem: "Archaeologists such as Hodges and Whitehouse, and later Michael McCormick" calls McCormick an archaeologist. Hodges and Whitehouse are archaeologists, but McCormick is a historian of the early medieval economy. He uses archaeological data, but a specialist would point out the label is wrong.
issues.fix: Change it to: "Scholars such as the archaeologists Hodges and Whitehouse, and later the historian Michael McCormick, have heavily revised it." This keeps the body within 22 to 40 words.

issues.problem: The risk notes say Scottish historians debate Trevor-Roper's Highland argument, but the slide's flag is empty. Other contested slides carry a flag, so this one should too.
issues.fix: Set the flag to "Debated". You can keep the body text as it is, because "largely constructed" is already attributed to Trevor-Roper.

issues.problem: "Seven ideas do more work in a historian's head than any list of dates" is a broad, unsourced claim. It is mild rhetoric but slightly overstated.
issues.fix: Change it to: "Seven ideas that help historians see patterns a list of dates cannot."
